front: Bar chart: what goes on which shelf?
back: A dimension on Rows and a measure on Columns, or vice versa. Dimension on Columns and measure on Rows gives vertical bars; the reverse gives horizontal bars.

front: With the mark type on Automatic, when does Tableau pick Bar?
back: "When there is a dimension and a measure as inner fields on Rows and Columns shelves."

front: Vertical or horizontal bars: which shelf holds the dimension?
back: Dimension on Columns and measure on Rows gives vertical bars. Dimension on Rows and measure on Columns gives horizontal bars.

front: What makes a bar chart easy to read as a ranking?
back: Sort the dimension by the measure (a computed sort, task 2.3).

front: Line chart: what goes on which shelf?
back: A date on Columns and a measure on Rows. With a date and a measure as the inner fields, Automatic chooses Line.

front: Continuous date vs. discrete date part on a line chart?
back: A continuous date value draws one line along a time axis. A discrete date part such as `YEAR(Start)` creates headers rather than an axis, and the line runs across the headers.

front: With the mark type on Automatic, when does Tableau pick Line?
back: "When there is a date field and a measure as the inner fields."

front: Why does a continuous date pill draw an axis?
back: Continuous dimensions visualize data with a linear, continuous axis. A discrete one draws headers.

front: Scatterplot: what goes on which shelf?
back: At least one measure on Columns and at least one measure on Rows. Add a dimension to Detail (or Color) to get one mark per member.

front: A scatterplot has two measures and no dimension in the view. How many marks?
back: One. Both measures are aggregated over all the data. Add a dimension to Detail for more marks.

front: A dimension on Columns or Rows of a scatterplot: what happens?
back: It creates panes of scatterplots, not more points in one plot. For more marks in one plot, put the dimension on Detail or Color.

front: Scatterplot is measure by what?
back: Measure by measure: a measure on each shelf.

front: Symbol (point) map: what goes where?
back: Longitude on Columns, Latitude on Rows, the geographic field on Detail: one mark per location. Add a measure to Size for a proportional symbol map.

front: Filled map: what goes where?
back: Select Map as the mark type, put a geographic dimension on Detail, and a measure or continuous dimension on Color.

front: `Latitude (generated)` and `Longitude (generated)`
back: Fields Tableau gives you when a field has a geographic role. Double-clicking them in the Data pane puts them on Rows and Columns.

front: Filled map vs. symbol map: which mark type and encoding?
back: Filled map: the Map mark type with the measure on Color. Symbol map: a circle or shape per location, usually with the measure on Size.

front: Combined axis chart
back: Two or more measures on one shared axis. Tableau's help calls it a blended axis.

front: How do you make a combined (blended) axis?
back: Drag one measure or axis and drop it onto an existing axis. Tableau replaces the measure with Measure Values and adds Measure Names to Color.

front: When do you use a combined axis?
back: For measures in the same units, such as Target Hours vs. Actual Hours, so one axis lets you compare them directly.

front: Combined axis: which two fields does Tableau use?
back: Measure Values on the shelf and Measure Names on Color. Each measure gets its own colour on the same scale.

front: Dual axis chart
back: Two measures layered in one view, each with its own axis: one on the left (or bottom) and one on the right (or top).

front: Two ways to make a dual axis chart
back: Drag the second measure to the right side of the view until a black dashed line appears. Or put both measures on Rows (or Columns), right-click one and select Dual Axis.

front: Dual axis: how many Marks cards, and why does it matter?
back: One Marks card per measure, so each measure can have its own mark type, like bars for one and a line for the other.

front: How do you put both axes of a dual axis on the same scale?
back: Right-click the secondary axis and select Synchronize Axis.

front: How many layered axes can a view have?
back: Up to four: two on the Columns shelf and two on the Rows shelf.

front: Combined axis vs. dual axis: how many axes, and best for?
back: Combined: one shared axis, for the same units. Dual: two independent axes (can be synchronized), for different units or scales.

front: Which has its own mark type per measure, a combined or a dual axis?
back: Only the dual axis. A combined axis uses one mark type for both measures.

front: Stacked bar: how do you build one?
back: Start with a bar chart and drag a second dimension to Color. Marks are automatically stacked.

front: Where do you control whether marks stack?
back: Analysis > Stack Marks. Choose Automatic, On or Off. The default is Automatic.

front: What does each segment of a stacked bar show?
back: Each bar splits into coloured segments, one per member of the Color dimension, and the segments add up to the bar's total.

front: Stacked bar: which shelf holds the second dimension?
back: Color on the Marks card.

front: Density map: what goes where?
back: Longitude on Columns, Latitude on Rows, a field with many underlying data points (such as an ID) on Detail, and the mark type set to Density.

front: How do you switch a view to the Density mark?
back: Open the mark type drop-down to the right of Automatic on the Marks card and select Density.

front: Density map: what do the Intensity slider and the palettes do?
back: Intensity increases or decreases the vividness of the map. You can choose from ten density colour palettes.

front: When is a density map the right choice?
back: For data with many overlapping points, to show where points cluster.

front: Crosstab (text table): what goes where?
back: One dimension on Rows, another on Columns, then drag one or more measures to Text on the Marks card.

front: Highlight table: what goes where?
back: Dimensions on Columns and Rows, Square as the mark type, and a measure of interest on Color. Keep the measure on Label too for the exact value.

front: Crosstab vs. highlight table: what differs?
back: A crosstab puts the measure on Text. A highlight table changes the mark type to Square and puts the measure on Color.

front: Crosstab
back: A text table, also called a cross-tab or pivot table. Use a table when readers need exact numbers rather than shapes.
